headline: GalaxEye Awards Bellatrix Aerospace Propulsion Contract for Its Next 30 Satellites
subheadline: The multi-year deal makes Bellatrix the primary propulsion supplier for GalaxEye's Drishti Gen-II imaging constellation — described by the two Bengaluru startups as India's largest private space order by satellite count.
body:
• Bengaluru-based GalaxEye has awarded Bellatrix Aerospace a multi-year contract to supply Arka electric propulsion systems for its next 30 Drishti Gen-II satellites.
  • The two startups describe it as India's largest order between private space companies by satellite count; the contract value was not disclosed.
  • Deliveries begin with systems for the first two satellites, with Bellatrix as the programme's primary propulsion supplier for a constellation GalaxEye aims to deploy by 2030.
  • The deal follows GalaxEye's loss of contact with its first satellite after a geomagnetic storm, and Bellatrix's $20 million pre-Series B round in March 2026.

Two Bengaluru startups have signed what they describe as the largest business-to-business order in India's private space sector by satellite count. GalaxEye, which builds Earth-imaging satellites, has awarded Bellatrix Aerospace a multi-year contract to design, build, test and deliver its Arka Hall-effect electric propulsion systems for GalaxEye's next 30 Drishti Gen-II satellites. The agreement was announced on Tuesday at the fifth India International Space Conclave in New Delhi, organised by the Indian Space Association (ISpA). The companies did not disclose the contract's value.

What the propulsion systems do

GalaxEye's satellites combine optical cameras and synthetic aperture radar on a single platform — its OptoSAR technology — to image the Earth through cloud cover and at night, for customers in defence, agriculture, disaster management, maritime monitoring and infrastructure. The Bellatrix thrusters will move each satellite from its drop-off orbit into its assigned position, hold spacing across the constellation, avoid space debris and deorbit the satellite at the end of its working life. Bellatrix's Arka thrusters use electric propulsion, which is more propellant-efficient than conventional chemical systems; the company flight-tested its propulsion technology aboard ISRO's PSLV-C58 POEM-3 mission in January 2024.

"The Indian private ecosystem is here and now, and it is time that we partner with each other and not just rely on the government."

— Pranit Mehta, co-founder, GalaxEye, to Inc42

GalaxEye co-founder Pranit Mehta told Inc42 that deliveries will begin with systems for the first two satellites before scaling to the full constellation, and that Bellatrix will be the programme's primary propulsion supplier. He said GalaxEye is also in active discussions with other Indian companies for power, control and communications subsystems.

Where each company stands

GalaxEye was founded in 2021 by Suyash Singh, Denil Chawda, Kishan Thakkar, Pranit Mehta and Rakshit Bhatt. Its first satellite, launched aboard a SpaceX Falcon 9 in May 2026 under Mission Drishti, validated deployment, attitude control and onboard computing before the company lost communication with it in July, following an anomaly it linked to a geomagnetic solar storm. The startup has since secured a US patent for its OptoSAR technology, received a commitment of ₹63.84 crore from the Technology Development Board, and acquired spacecraft engineering company StarOps. Bellatrix Aerospace, founded in 2015 by Rohan M. Ganapathy and Yashas Karanam, raised $20 million in a pre-Series B round led by Cactus Partners in March 2026 and is expanding its manufacturing capacity, according to India Today and Inc42.

The wider pattern at the conclave

The contract was one of several domestic partnerships announced at the conclave: Earth-observation startup Pixxel signed memoranda of understanding with Centum Electronics and CS TECH Ai covering satellite payload electronics and geospatial applications. For India's private space sector, the GalaxEye order is the pattern worth watching — a satellite operator buying a critical subsystem from another Indian startup at constellation scale, rather than importing it or waiting on a government programme. The test now is delivery: the first two propulsion systems ship first, and the 30-satellite constellation is a 2030 target, not a fleet in orbit.
diaspora_angle: India's private space sector is maturing into a domestic supply chain, with startups now selling constellation-scale hardware to each other.

key_takeaways: GalaxEye awards Bellatrix Aerospace a contract for 30 satellites' propulsion systems.
This is India's largest satellite order between private space companies.
Deliveries for the first two satellites will begin soon.
GalaxEye aims to deploy its satellite constellation by 2030.
Bellatrix's propulsion systems are more efficient than traditional chemical systems.
